title: Two Sum
directAnswer: Return the indices (not values) of the two numbers that sum to target. Brute force is O(n²); the canonical answer is a single-pass hash map storing value → index, checking complement = target − current before inserting.

rules: Return **indices**, not values — the most common misread of this prompt.
Check `target − x` in the map **before** inserting `x`. Flipping those two lines silently breaks `[3, 3], target = 6`.
Store `value → index`, never `index → value` — you need `O(1)` membership on the value.
In Python use `complement in seen`, not `if seen.get(complement):` — a stored index of `0` is falsy.
Brute force first, **then** optimal. Interviewers grade for the progression, not just the final answer.

remember.takeaway: Hash-map complement lookup is the interview-grade trick for turning pair-finding into membership testing. Once you see it, you'll spot it in Subarray Sum Equals K, 3Sum, Group Anagrams, and LRU Cache — it's one pattern, many problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a hash map on 'find a pair' over an unsorted array — and whether you derive that from brute force instead of jumping straight to the answer.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning values [2, 7] instead of indices [0, 1], or inserting into the map before checking the complement (silently wrong on nums = [3, 3], target = 6).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State brute force first, then 'we can do better'. Name the pattern (complement lookup) and mention it shows up in Subarray Sum K, 3Sum, Two Sum II.

problemStatement:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return **the indices** of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input would have ***exactly one solution***, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.
understanding: Find two distinct positions whose values sum to target — return positions, not values. Duplicates are allowed (same value at two different indices is a valid pair).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. If it were, two pointers would beat the hash map (that's Two Sum II).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — nums = [3, 3], target = 6 must return [0, 1]. Handled correctly only by checking the map before inserting.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can numbers be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Don't write code that assumes positive values.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Indices or values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Indices. The word 'numbers' in the prompt is the trap that makes candidates return values.

examples.explanation: Same value at two different indices — both are valid.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Nested Pair Scan
approaches.whenToMention: Always say this first to show structured thinking — never skip straight to the optimal.
hints: The problem guarantees exactly one answer — that means there is some pair (i, j) with i < j whose values add up to target. What's the simplest way to find such a pair?
Try every ordered pair (i, j) with j > i. For each pair, check whether nums[i] + nums[j] == target.
Two nested loops: outer over i from 0 to n-1, inner over j from i+1 to n-1. Return [i, j] the moment the sum matches.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 comparisons in the worst case; no extra data structures.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal translation of the question into code: for every index `i`, walk every later index `j > i` and test whether `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`. Return the first pair that matches.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem asks for *two* indices that sum to `target`. The obvious question to ask in a nested loop is exactly the question the problem asked — one pointer fixes the first number, the other pointer tries every candidate second number. No clever insight needed, just mechanical enumeration.

**Why `j = i + 1` and not `j = 0`.** If `j` started at `0`, we'd do two bad things: pair `i` with itself when `i == j` (producing false matches on even targets like `nums[i] + nums[i] == 2*nums[i]`), and re-check the same unordered pair twice — once as `(i, j)` and again as `(j, i)`. Starting `j` at `i + 1` fixes both problems for free: every unordered pair is visited exactly once, and self-pairing is impossible.

**Why we don't ship this.** The total work is `n + (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 ≈ n²/2`. For `n = 10⁴` (the constraint) that's ~50 million comparisons — fast enough to *pass* Two Sum, but you're telling the interviewer you can't see the better answer. Mention this approach, state its cost, then reach for the hash map.
approaches.insight: Starting `j` at `i + 1` does double duty: it prevents pairing an index with itself, and it skips checking `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` separately. That's the first micro-optimization every candidate should state — it shows you think about loop invariants, not just syntax.

approaches.name: Hash Map — One Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'check if the complement was already seen' — not just 'use a hash map'.
hints: If you knew, for each number x, whether target − x was somewhere else in the array, the problem would be trivial. What data structure answers 'have I seen this value before?' in O(1)?
Use a hash map keyed by value, valued by index. As you scan left-to-right, for each num compute complement = target − num and check the map before inserting.
If the complement is in the map, you've found your pair: return [map.get(complement), currentIndex]. Otherwise, put (num → currentIndex) into the map and continue. One pass, no second loop.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass × O(1) average map ops = O(n) time. Map holds up to n−1 entries → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the array exactly once. At each position compute `complement = target − nums[i]`. If the complement has already been seen, return `[seen[complement], i]`. Otherwise record `seen[nums[i]] = i` and continue.

**The mental shift that unlocks this.** Brute force asks *"does this pair sum to target?"* for every pair — that's quadratic because there are `n²/2` pairs. The hash map re-frames the question: for any single element `x`, the partner that would complete the pair is *uniquely determined* as `target − x`. So instead of enumerating pairs, we enumerate elements and ask one yes/no question per element: *"have I already seen `target − x`?"* A hash map answers that in `O(1)` average, so `n` elements × `O(1)` questions = `O(n)` time.

**Why the insert happens after the check.** The single most important line ordering in this algorithm is this: **look up first, insert second**. Consider `nums = [3, 3], target = 6`. On `i = 0` we compute `complement = 3`. If we inserted first, the map would already contain `3 → 0`, the lookup would succeed, and we'd return `[0, 0]` — matching the element against *itself*. By doing the lookup on an empty map at `i = 0`, then inserting `3 → 0`, the second `3` at `i = 1` finds the earlier one at index `0` and correctly returns `[0, 1]`. Same three lines of code, wrong order, silent bug.

**Why `value → index` and not the reverse.** The question we ask each step is *"is this *value* one I've seen?"* Hash maps give `O(1)` lookup only on the key, so the thing we look up has to be the key. Indices as keys would force us to scan the map every step — `O(n)` per step, `O(n²)` total — and we'd be back where we started.

**Why we stop at the first match.** The problem guarantees *exactly one* valid pair, so returning on the first hit is both correct and optimal. If the problem said *"return all pairs"*, we'd keep going and append instead of returning.
approaches.insight: The whole algorithm is a single *trade*: we pay `O(n)` extra memory to buy `O(1)` answers to the question "seen this value before?". Memory-for-time is the default trade in algorithm design — when you're stuck on a quadratic pair/triple/match problem, ask what you could *remember* to skip work, and a hash map is usually the answer. This exact shape recurs in Subarray Sum Equals K (remember prefix sums), Longest Consecutive Sequence (remember elements), and LRU Cache (remember recency).

pitfalls: Inserting before checking — silently wrong on duplicates like [3, 3], target = 6.
Storing index → value instead of value → index — makes the lookup O(n).
In Python, `if seen.get(complement):` is falsy when the stored index is 0 — use `in seen`.

commonMistakes: Returning the values [2, 7] instead of the indices [0, 1].
Inserting into the hash map BEFORE checking the complement — wrong on duplicates.
Sorting the input to use two pointers — destroys the original index mapping.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning values instead of indices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The prompt says 'indices' but the brain reads 'numbers'. Re-read the output spec before coding.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Insert before check (duplicate trap)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On nums = [3, 3], target = 6, insert-first puts 3→0 in the map and the same iteration's complement lookup matches it — returning [0, 0].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Python truthiness on stored zero
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the stored index is 0, `if seen.get(complement):` evaluates to falsy and the check incorrectly fails. Always use `in seen`.

if complement in seen:
